316.title: The boy who asked what dies
316.hook: a sixteen-year-old in Madurai lies down on the floor and acts out his own death
316.carry: who am i? the self, not the body
316.tomorrow: karma: seva, and a word Ramakrishna refused
316.howItsDone: Visitors to Ramana Maharshi's ashram at Tiruvannamalai sit in silence in his old hall and walk around the hill of Arunachala; followers practice self-inquiry by turning attention to the sense of I rather than to its thoughts.

segments.voice: Last week closed on three roads: karma with Vivekananda, bhakti with Jayadeva's Gita Govinda, jnana with I am Brahman. in bhakti, love runs both ways: sometimes God bows. This week, a new teacher on the jnana road.
screen: `IN BHAKTI, LOVE RUNS BOTH WAYS: SOMETIMES GOD BOWS.`

segments.voice: Madurai, South India, the summer of 1896. A sixteen-year-old boy named Venkataraman is alone in a room in his uncle's house. He's healthy. Nothing is wrong. Suddenly an overwhelming fear hits him: he's about to die. He could call someone, or go for a walk. He does something else. He lies down on the floor, stretches out his limbs like a corpse, holds his breath, and says to himself: all right. Death has come. What does it mean? What is it that's dying?
screen: `MADURAI, 1896.` → `A SUDDEN FEAR OF DEATH.` → `HE LIES DOWN AND ASKS.`

segments.voice: Lying there, as he later told it, he reasoned it through. This body is dead. They'll carry it to the cremation ground and burn it. But with the body dead, am I dead? Is the body I? And in that moment, he said, he knew directly that he was not the body. The fear vanished and never came back. He hadn't studied any of this, he said later, but Hindus have an old name for what he found: the atman, the Self. The Gita puts it plainly: the body is born and dies; the Self is not born and does not die. A few weeks later he left home with a short note and took a train toward a sacred mountain called Arunachala, in the town of Tiruvannamalai. He stayed there more than fifty years. People came to call him Ramana Maharshi, and they came from far away just to sit with him. When he did teach, the heart of it was one question: who am I? Not I'm a student, I'm a parent, I'm tired. Those are things you have, he'd say, in effect, not what you are. Follow the feeling of I back to where it comes from. That's self-inquiry: the jnana road with almost nothing extra. So when the world sums you up in one label, the grade, the job, the mistake, this is the Hindu answer: the atman isn't any of those. Ask who am I, and look.
screen: `THE BODY DIES. AM I DEAD?` · `THE FEAR NEVER CAME BACK.` · `THE ATMAN: NOT BORN, NOT DYING.` · `ONE QUESTION: WHO AM I?` · then, large: `THE SELF, NOT THE BODY.`

segments.voice: Ask the question once, quietly: who am I? Don't answer with a name or a role; just notice the plain sense of being here, this I that's listening, and when a thought comes, let it pass and come back to the question. Rest in the space where the answer would be; it's fine if nothing happens, because the looking is the practice, and if you pray, you can rest in God as the source of that I.
Karma, action, is the word these weeks carry. Ramana's action was to lie down and look, and he spent his life inviting others to look too.
Your line: who am I? The Self, not the body. Not a name, not a label: the one asking. See you tomorrow.

317.title: Serve every being as Shiva
317.hook: a teacher hears the word compassion and stops the room: who are you to be compassionate?
317.tomorrow: bhakti: Radha in the spring forest
317.howItsDone: Seva is practiced in Hindu temples as service to the deity and to devotees, cleaning, cooking and serving food, and the Ramakrishna Mission and many other Hindu organizations run hospitals, schools and relief work as seva, serving people as God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the jnana road: Ramana Maharshi, sixteen, on the floor, asking who am I. Today the karma road reaches its last stretch: seva as a life.

A charity photo: someone well dressed hands a meal to someone who isn't. Both smile for the camera, and the picture still says who's above and who's below. Now a temple garden at Dakshineswar, near Calcutta, in the 1880s. A small group of young men sits around their teacher, Ramakrishna, and someone mentions a teaching about showing compassion to all living beings. It sounds beautiful. And Ramakrishna, the story goes, stops the room.
screen: `THE CHARITY PHOTO.` → `A TEMPLE GARDEN, THE 1880S.` → `RAMAKRISHNA STOPS THE ROOM.`

segments.voice: Compassion to beings? he says. Who are you to show compassion? You, a tiny creature, being kind to others as if from above? No. Not compassion. Service. Serve every being as Shiva himself. In Bengali the phrase is often given as shiva jnane jiva seva: serving living beings, knowing them as God. In the room was a young man named Narendranath, who would become Swami Vivekananda. As his fellow disciples told it, he walked out afterward and said something like: I've found a great light today, and if God lets me, I'll proclaim it everywhere. And he did. When he founded the Ramakrishna Mission, he gave it a motto that joins two things: for one's own liberation, and for the good of the world. The word seva is older than any of them, from a Sanskrit root that means to attend on, to honor, to serve. In a temple, seva is what you do for the image of God: bathing it, dressing it, offering food. Ramakrishna pointed that same word outward. The hungry person in front of you gets the same care as the image in the shrine. Now look at the charity photo again. There's no above and below. The one serving stands where a worshiper stands. Seva isn't volunteering on the side of your spiritual life. On the karma road, it is the spiritual life.
screen: `WHO ARE YOU TO SHOW COMPASSION?` · `SERVE EVERY BEING AS SHIVA.` · `A YOUNG MAN SAW A GREAT LIGHT.` · `NO ABOVE, NO BELOW.` · then, large: `SHIVA JNANE JIVA SEVA.`

segments.voice: Think of someone you'll likely help today in any small way, a kid, a coworker, a stranger at a counter, an aging parent, and notice any feeling of being above them, even slightly: the helper, the one who has it together. Let it go with the out-breath, and picture serving them the way you'd offer something at a shrine: carefully, gladly, as if it were an honor. If you pray, you can ask to see God in them.
Karma. Action. On the karma road's last stretch, the action is seva: service offered to beings as if to God.
Your line: serve every being as Shiva. Ramakrishna carried a temple word out into the street. Day three hundred seventeen.

318.title: The friend between them
318.hook: spring in the forest, Radha sees Krishna dancing with everyone else, and a friend steps in
318.carry: god searches for the soul too
318.tomorrow: jnana: to whom did this thought come?
318.howItsDone: The Gita Govinda's songs are sung in temples and at home, and its opening hymn to Vishnu's ten avatars is often sung on its own; in Vaishnava traditions devotees honor the sakhis, Radha's friends, as models of selfless devotion.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the karma road: seva, not compassion from above, but serve every being as Shiva. Today, back into Jayadeva's poem.

Someone walks into a party looking for one person, and there they are: laughing, surrounded, completely fine. Nobody did anything wrong, exactly. But leaving suddenly looks easier than staying. That's where Jayadeva's poem puts Radha. It's spring in the forest by the Yamuna. Bees, blossoms, a warm wind from the south. Radha's friend leads her to a clearing and points: there's Krishna, dancing and playing with all the other gopis.
screen: `LOOKING FOR ONE PERSON.` → `SPRING BY THE YAMUNA.` → `KRISHNA, WITH EVERYONE ELSE.`

segments.voice: Radha doesn't make a scene. She withdraws, alone into a thicket of vines, hurt and jealous and full of longing all at once. Then the poem does something interesting. Krishna, in the middle of the dance, suddenly remembers her. He leaves the others to look for her, can't find her, and now he's the miserable one. So they're apart, each longing for the other, and neither can simply walk across the forest and fix it. That's when Radha's friend, the sakhi, gets to work. She goes to Krishna and describes Radha's grief. She goes back to Radha and tells her how Krishna is suffering. Back and forth, carrying the messages, softening the hurt, until the two can meet again. Devotees hear layers in this. Krishna dancing with everyone is God's love for all souls. Radha's hurt is the soul feeling, for a moment, like one among many. Krishna's search says God is not fine without you after all. That's a core bhakti teaching: the love runs both ways, and God goes looking for the soul too. And the sakhi? In some Vaishnava traditions, devotees see her as the model of what a teacher or a community does: the friend who carries messages between the soul and God. Some traditions go further and hope for nothing more than to be that friend, serving the love between Radha and Krishna. One more thing: the poem opens with a hymn to Vishnu's ten descents into the world, and people still sing it on its own.
screen: `RADHA WITHDRAWS, HURT.` · `KRISHNA LEAVES THE DANCE TO FIND HER.` · `THE FRIEND CARRIES THE MESSAGES.` · `GOD IS NOT FINE WITHOUT YOU.` · then, large: `GOD SEARCHES FOR THE SOUL TOO.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who once carried a message for you: a friend who explained you to someone you'd hurt, a teacher who helped you back to something you'd lost, a grandparent who made peace in the family, and thank them silently. Then, as devotees on this road do, say one name of God you love, Krishna, Rama, Shiva, or simply God, once and slowly, as if answering someone already looking for you. If you don't pray, just rest in the thought that you're being looked for.
Karma, action, is the word these weeks carry. In the Gita Govinda, the action that heals is the friend's: going back and forth until two can meet.
Your line: God searches for the soul too. Radha hid, Krishna searched, and a friend went back and forth. That's three hundred eighteen days.

319.title: To whom did this thought come?
319.hook: a silent young swami on Arunachala writes out his answers for a visitor
319.carry: trace each thought back to the self
319.tomorrow: karma: the king who gave away his last meal
319.howItsDone: People who follow Ramana Maharshi's teaching practice self-inquiry in daily life and in silent sitting, turning each thought back with the question 'to whom?'; many combine it with devotion, as Ramana allowed.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the bhakti road: Radha hurt in the spring forest, and Krishna searching. God searches for the soul too. Today, Ramana's method, up close.

Around 1902, a visitor named Sivaprakasam Pillai climbs the hill of Arunachala to a cave where a young swami lives. That's Ramana, still in his early twenties. Pillai has brought a list of questions, but in those years Ramana hardly speaks. So he answers in writing. The first question on the list is the one Ramana asked himself at sixteen, on that floor: who am I? Pillai keeps the answers, and they become a small book, Nan Yar?, Who Am I? One of its moves is about what happens the second any of us sits still: a thought shows up.
screen: `ARUNACHALA, AROUND 1902.` → `A SILENT SWAMI WRITES HIS ANSWERS.` → `FIRST QUESTION: WHO AM I?`

segments.voice: Your mind plans dinner. Then it replays something someone said on Tuesday. Most advice gives two options: fight the thought, or follow it. Ramana's answers offer a third. Don't chase it, and don't wrestle it. Ask: to whom did this thought come? The answer comes back instantly: to me. Then ask: and who am I? In that moment the attention turns around. Instead of flowing out toward dinner or Tuesday, it flows back toward its own source, and the thought drops away, because nobody's feeding it. His reasoning: of all thoughts, the thought I is the first. Every other thought is a thought to someone: I'm hungry, I'm annoyed, I remember. Trace I back, and every other thought loses its root. Ramana called this atma-vichara, inquiry into the Self: the same atman the boy found on the floor. He gave a picture from the cremation ground. A stick stirs the cremation fire, and at the end the stick itself is thrown into the flames. The question who am I works like that stick: it burns away the other thoughts, and in the end it burns away too, leaving only what was there all along. Ramana was generous about other roads. If you can't inquire, he said, surrender completely to God; both lead to the same place. And it's portable: no temple, no book. The next time a thought won't let you sleep, one question.
screen: `TO WHOM DID THIS THOUGHT COME? TO ME.` · `AND WHO AM I?` · `ATMA-VICHARA: INQUIRY INTO THE SELF.` · `THE STICK THAT STIRS THE FIRE BURNS TOO.` · then, large: `TO WHOM?`

segments.voice: Let thoughts come as they will, and when one appears, don't push it away or follow it; ask quietly: to whom did this come? To me. And who am I? Let the attention rest wherever it lands, without needing an answer, and ask again with the next thought; ten times in two minutes is the practice working. If surrender suits you better, as Ramana allowed, you can simply hand each thought to God instead.
Karma, action, is the word these weeks carry. Ramana's action is the smallest one on the path: one question, turned back toward the one who asks.
Your line: trace each thought back to the Self. One question does it: to whom? Day three hundred nineteen, done.

screen: `DAY 319 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: KARMA — THE KING WHO GAVE HIS LAST MEAL.`

320.title: Rantideva's last meal
320.hook: a starving king gives his last meal and water to whoever knocks
320.carry: give with faith; the guest is god
320.howItsDone: Many Hindu homes treat a guest as God (atithi devo bhava), feed whoever arrives and set aside food before a meal; dana, giving, is a daily and festival duty, and Gita 17.20–22 and the Taittiriya Upanishad's 'give with faith' are often quoted on how a gift should be given.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the jnana road: trace each thought back to the Self by asking, to whom? Today the karma road, and seva as a whole life, starting with how you give.

A king named Rantideva has given away so much that he and his family have nothing left. The Bhagavata Purana says they went forty-eight days without food, and without even water. On the forty-ninth morning, someone brings them a little: rice cooked in milk, some ghee, some water. They sit down to eat at last. And there's a knock. A guest is at the door, and he's hungry.
screen: `FORTY-EIGHT DAYS WITHOUT FOOD.` → `THE FORTY-NINTH MORNING.` → `A KNOCK AT THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: Rantideva shares his food with the guest, honoring him. Then a second guest comes, a poor laborer, and he shares again. Then a man arrives with a pack of hungry dogs, and Rantideva gives him the rest of the food and bows to the man and the dogs alike. Only the water is left. Then an outcaste comes, a man the society of that time wouldn't even touch, and says he's dying of thirst. Rantideva, nearly dying of thirst himself, gives him the water. The Purana gives him a prayer at that moment: he doesn't ask God for powers, or even for freedom from rebirth; he asks to take on the pain of every creature, so that they can be free of it. Then the guests show who they really were: the lords of the three worlds, come to test him. He bows, and he asks them for nothing. That's dana, giving, as Hindu texts hold it up. The Taittiriya Upanishad, in its parting advice to students, says: treat the guest as God, atithi devo bhava. A line later: give with faith. The Gita's seventeenth chapter sorts gifts three ways. The clear gift is given because giving is right, to someone who can't repay you. The restless gift wants something back, or comes with a wince. The heavy gift comes with contempt. It's why so many Hindu homes won't let a guest leave hungry. Today the guest is your kid's friend at dinner, the new coworker, the driver at your door: the same welcome, no bill attached.
screen: `A GUEST. A LABORER. A MAN WITH DOGS.` · `THE LAST WATER, TO AN OUTCASTE.` · `HE ASKED FOR NOTHING.` · `ATITHI DEVO BHAVA: THE GUEST IS GOD.` · then, large: `ŚRADDHAYĀ DEYAM.`

segments.voice: Picture the next meal you'll eat. Many Hindu homes set aside a little food before anyone eats: for a guest, a hungry person, a cow, the birds. Decide where a first portion of yours could go this week, a meal, an hour, a seat at your table, and who might receive it. If you pray, offer the meal to God first, as Rantideva saw God in each guest; if you don't, give quiet thanks for whoever it reaches.
Karma. Action. Rantideva's action was the simplest gift there is: his own meal, given to whoever knocked, asking nothing back.
Your line: give with faith; the guest is God. Rantideva gave his last meal and asked for nothing. See you tomorrow.

321.title: Krishna fixes Radha's hair
321.hook: the love poem ends not with a wedding but with God fixing his beloved's hair
321.carry: in bhakti, god serves the one who loves
321.tomorrow: Arjuna asks which road is best
321.howItsDone: The Gita Govinda has long been sung in the worship of Jagannath at Puri and is performed in Odissi and other classical dance and music; in homes and temples devotees bathe and dress the murti each day (shringar), and hear the poem's reunion as God's love for the soul.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the karma road: Rantideva's last meal. Give with faith; the guest is God. Today, the bhakti road's last day with Jayadeva.

A wedding. A kiss in the rain. Credits roll. That's where a lot of love stories stop. Jayadeva's Gita Govinda ends somewhere much quieter. After the hurt and the searching and the messages carried back and forth, after Krishna has pleaded with Radha to forgive him, she finally comes to him in the forest bower at night. And in the poem's very last song, the morning after, Radha asks Krishna for something small. Fix my hair, she says. Put my ornaments back. And he does.
screen: `NOT A WEDDING. NOT CREDITS.` → `RADHA COMES TO THE BOWER.` → `FIX MY HAIR, SHE SAYS.`

segments.voice: Here is the Lord of the universe, the cowherd whose flute the gopis ran to, the child who showed the whole cosmos in his mouth, sitting in the grass, carefully drawing the line of dark makeup around Radha's eyes, pinning flowers back into her hair, fastening her anklets. That's the poem's last image. Remember the line tradition says Jayadeva hesitated to write, where Krishna asks Radha to put her foot on his head? The ending finishes that thought. On the bhakti road, God isn't only the one who is served. God serves. In the reunion, the Lord does seva for the one who loves him. This week the karma road has been about seva: serving every being as God. In the Gita Govinda, God serves the soul. The service goes both ways. The poem didn't stay on the page. Tradition says its songs were sung in worship at the Jagannath temple in Puri, and temple dancers performed them; Odissi dancers still do. Singers perform its songs, the ashtapadis, each one built of eight verses. And you can see this teaching in Hindu homes every morning. Someone bathes the murti, the image of God in the family shrine, and dresses it: fresh clothes, flowers, a little jewelry. It's called shringar. Devotees read the poem's ending as the other half of that love: the God you dress and adorn is the God who once pinned flowers back into Radha's hair.
screen: `THE LORD FIXES RADHA'S HAIR.` · `SEVA GOES BOTH WAYS.` · `SUNG IN WORSHIP AT PURI.` · `SHRINGAR: DRESSING THE MURTI.` · then, large: `GOD SERVES THE ONE WHO LOVES.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who once tended to you in a small, physical way: brushed your hair when you were little, fixed your collar before something important, brought you soup. Picture their hands, and receive that care again as you breathe in. Then, if you keep a shrine, offer one small act of care today: a flower, a fresh cloth, a lamp. If you don't pray, tend one person you love in a small way, as an offering.
Karma, action, is the word these weeks carry, and the Gita Govinda ends with a small, gentle action: God tending the one he loves.
Your line: in bhakti, God serves the one who loves. The poem ends on flowers pinned back in her hair. That's day three hundred twenty-one.

322.title: Arjuna asks which road
322.hook: Arjuna begs Krishna to name the one right way, and Krishna won't split them
322.carry: only the childish split the paths
322.tomorrow: guided visits: what a Sikh means by seva
322.howItsDone: Hindus often speak of three great paths: karma (selfless action), bhakti (devotion) and jnana (knowledge). People often lean toward one, and some teachers say the paths meet; schools differ on how.

segments.voice: Yesterday: in bhakti, God serves the one who loves, as Krishna fixed Radha's hair. Today the three tracks end: karma, bhakti, jnana.

The battlefield of the Bhagavad Gita. Arjuna has heard Krishna praise two ways: giving up action to seek knowledge, and acting without craving for the fruit. He's confused, and he's honest about it. At the start of the fifth chapter he says, in effect: you praise both. Tell me for certain which one is better. Just one. It's the question anyone asks when a tradition offers too many doors: which is the real way?
screen: `ARJUNA IS CONFUSED.` → `WHICH ONE IS BETTER?` → `JUST TELL ME ONE.`

segments.voice: Krishna's answer surprises him. Both lead to the highest good, he says, though of the two, acting without craving is the better. Then comes the line Hindus still quote: it's the childish, not the wise, who speak of knowledge and action as separate. Settle into either one, and you reach what both reach. Some teachers hear that as true of all three roads you've walked these three weeks. The kitchen: the karma road ended with seva as a life, a king giving his last meal and asking nothing back. The song: the bhakti road ended with the Gita Govinda, God searching for the soul and, at the end, tending it. The question: the jnana road ended with Ramana Maharshi on his hill, tracing each thought back to the Self. Hindus have argued for centuries about how these fit, and schools still disagree; this path doesn't settle it. But look at many Hindu families and you'll see all three under one roof: a grandmother at the shrine before breakfast, a father who calls his volunteering seva, a teenager who sits quietly and asks who she is. That isn't confusion. Many teachers would say it's what Krishna told Arjuna. And notice the word under all three: karma, from a root meaning to do. The ladle is a doing. The song is a doing. Even the question is a doing.
screen: `BOTH LEAD TO THE HIGHEST GOOD.` · `ONLY THE CHILDISH SPLIT THEM.` · `THE KITCHEN, THE SONG, THE QUESTION.` · `ALL THREE UNDER ONE ROOF.` · then, large: `KARMA: ALL THREE ARE A DOING.`

segments.voice: Let the track you walked come back to you: for the kitchen, one piece of work you did this month for someone else; for the song, a line or a name of God you love; for the question, let the word I rise and gently look for where it comes from. If you pray, offer all three to God, as the Gita asks you to offer every action. No grade, no finish line.
Karma. Action, from the Sanskrit root kri, to do. The first name on three tracks, and the ground under them all.
Your line: only the childish split the paths. Arjuna wanted one road; Krishna gave him the whole hill. Day three hundred twenty-two: three tracks, done.
